659.title: The gold-washer
659.hook: gold refined from coarse to fine impurities, step by step (AN 3, the gold-washer)
659.howItsDone: Buddhist training in many traditions is taught as gradual, beginning with ethical conduct and moving to meditation and wisdom, and teachers often use the gold-washer to describe that order.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of the Kalama talk, and your line, four comforts. Did a kind act settle something? Today the Book of Threes takes us to a riverbank, where a man is washing dirt for gold. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

If you've ever cleaned out a garage, you know the order. First the big stuff: the broken bike, the boxes of who knows what. Then the medium stuff: tools, cans, things to sort. Then the fine stuff: dust, cobwebs, the last screws in the corner. Nobody starts with the cobwebs while the bike's still in the way. The Buddha used a picture like that, from a trade everyone in his world would have seen at work: someone standing in a river, washing gravel to find gold. Today: the gold-washer.
screen: `CLEANING OUT A GARAGE.` → `BIG STUFF FIRST, THEN DUST.` → `A MAN WASHING GRAVEL FOR GOLD.`

segments.voice: In this discourse from the Book of Threes, the Buddha describes the work step by step. Raw gold, he says, has coarse impurities: soil, sand, grit and gravel. The gold-washer pours it into a trough and washes and rinses them away. Then there are medium impurities: fine grit and coarse sand. He washes those out too. Then fine impurities: fine sand and black dust. Those go. What's left is gold dust. The goldsmith puts it in a crucible and blows on it, again and again. At first it isn't workable. It hasn't let go of all its dross. Then, at last, it becomes soft, pliable, bright, and ready for any ornament he wants, a ring, earrings, a chain. Then the Buddha maps it onto a person in training. The coarse impurities are misconduct of body, speech and mind. Those go first. The medium ones are thoughts of craving, ill will and harming. Then the fine ones: thoughts about one's family, one's home country, one's reputation. Then even thoughts about the teaching itself, a kind of busy spiritual chatter, are let go. And then the mind becomes steady, unified, and workable, like the gold. It's an honest picture of change. The order is practical: you don't work on subtle thoughts while you're still lying to people. And the pace is slow. Each stage gets its own washing. Nobody expects the whole riverbed to turn to gold in one pass. Even the last step, the crucible, takes time. The gold doesn't come out bright until it has let go of what isn't gold.
screen: `COARSE, MEDIUM, FINE IMPURITIES` · `GOLD DUST IN THE CRUCIBLE` · `BODY, SPEECH, MIND, THEN THOUGHTS` · `SOFT, BRIGHT, READY TO WORK` · then, large: `REFINED SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and choose one habit you'd like to refine. Not to remove all at once: to refine. Ask, like the gold-washer: what's the coarse part? Maybe it's the action itself: the sharp word, the extra drink, the late night. Picture washing just that layer away this week. You don't need to touch the finer layers yet, the thoughts and moods underneath. They'll come in their own time. Hold the one coarse step in mind, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
The gold-washer. In the Book of Threes, gold is washed of coarse, then medium, then fine impurities, and the mind is refined the same way, step by step. Today's word.
Your line: refined slowly. Work on the coarsest layer of one habit today, and leave the fine dust for later. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

myth: the gold-washer starts with the finest dust
he washes out the coarse impurities first, then the medium, then the fine.
the gold is workable as soon as it reaches the crucible
at first it isn't; only after repeated blowing does it become soft and bright.
thoughts about the teaching itself are among the last to settle
the discourse lists them after thoughts of family, country and reputation.

fork.setup: you're starting to train your mind, and there's a lot to work on. what does the gold-washer teach about where to start?
options: with the subtlest thoughts first.
with the coarse layer: misconduct of body, speech and mind.
all at once, in one pass.
fork.reveal: the coarse impurities go first, then the medium, then the fine. each stage gets its own washing.

original.note: Pali suvanna: gold, the metal refined in the gold-washer simile.

trapdoor: what you thought: the gold-washer is a picture of getting rid of bad habits.
what it means: in the Book of Threes, gold refined from coarse to medium to fine impurities, matched step by step to a mind refined in training.

what a scholar hears: the passage pairs with the next discourse, where a goldsmith balances blowing, sprinkling water and simply watching, the Buddha's image for balancing effort, concentration and equanimity.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.100 (Pamsudhovaka Sutta; AN 3.101 in some editions)

660.title: Salt in the river
660.hook: a lump of salt ruins a cup of water but is lost in the Ganges: a broad heart (AN 3, the salt crystal)
660.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the salt simile to explain that karma is not a mechanical tit-for-tat, and many practitioners develop the immeasurables, kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, to widen the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gold-washer, and your line, refined slowly. Which coarse layer did you wash? Today, the discourse just before it in the Book of Threes, and a pinch of salt. Day six hundred sixty.

Someone says one thoughtless thing to two different people. The first stews on it for a week, replays it at night, and tells three friends. The second barely notices, says huh, and carries on. Same words, same weight. Very different results. Why? People in the Buddha's time asked a sharper version of that question about karma. If every act brings back exactly what it deserves, measure for measure, how could anyone ever get free? The Buddha answered with something from the kitchen. Today: salt in the river.
screen: `ONE THOUGHTLESS REMARK.` → `TWO VERY DIFFERENT RESULTS.` → `AN ANSWER FROM THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: The discourse begins with a claim the Buddha rejects. If someone says, however a person acts, in exactly that way they'll experience the result, then, he says, there would be no living the holy life, no chance to make a complete end of suffering. Then the picture. Suppose someone drops a lump of salt into a small cup of water. Would the water become salty and undrinkable? Yes, sir. Because the cup is small. Now suppose they drop the same lump of salt into the river Ganges. Would the river become salty and undrinkable? No, sir. Because the Ganges is a great mass of water. The same small bad deed, he says, can lead one person to great suffering and barely touch another. The difference is in the person. One is undeveloped in body, in conduct, in mind, in wisdom: limited, small-hearted, living with suffering. The other is developed, not limited, great-hearted, dwelling in the immeasurable. For them, the result of that same small act is felt here and now, and not even a trace may appear beyond. He adds a second picture, almost a court case: one person is jailed for stealing a tiny coin, another, rich and powerful, isn't jailed for the same amount. It's not a teaching that small harms don't matter. The salt is still salt. It's a teaching that the size of the heart changes what the salt does. And it's hopeful: hearts can grow. A practice of kindness and wisdom isn't only about avoiding new salt. It's about becoming a river.
screen: `NOT EXACTLY AS YOU ACT, YOU REAP` · `A CUP OF WATER: UNDRINKABLE` · `THE GANGES: STILL CLEAR` · `THE SIZE OF THE HEART` · then, large: `SALT IN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and recall one small thing that's been bothering you: a comment, a mistake, a slight. Feel how salty it tastes in a small cup. Now let the cup widen. Breathe into the chest and imagine the heart as wide as a river, moving, full, room for many things. Bring in people you love, the sky, this whole morning. Then place that small salty thing into all of it, and watch how much less it dominates the taste. The bell holds the time.
Salt in the river. In the Book of Threes, a lump of salt ruins a small cup of water but is lost in the Ganges: a small deed weighs differently in a broad, developed heart. Today's word.
Your line: salt in the river. When something small stings today, widen your heart before you react, and let the river take it. Day six hundred sixty.

match.prompt: the salt crystal: tap the pairs.

fork.setup: someone asks you: if every act brings back exactly what it deserves, how can anyone get free? what does the Buddha answer?
options: nobody can.
a lump of salt ruins a cup but is lost in the Ganges.

fork.reveal: the same small deed weighs differently depending on the heart it falls into, so freedom is possible.

original.note: Pali lona: salt. the discourse is the Lonakapalla Sutta, the lump of salt.

trapdoor: what you thought: salt in the river means small problems don't matter.
what it means: in the Book of Threes, the same small deed weighs heavily in a limited heart and lightly in a developed, broad one.

what a scholar hears: the sutta is a key text against a mechanical reading of kamma, where every act must return in kind; it pairs the salt with a legal image of unequal punishment for the same small theft.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.99 (Lonakapalla Sutta; AN 3.100 in some editions)

661.title: Three intoxications
661.hook: the pride of youth, of health, of life (AN 3.38)
661.howItsDone: Many Buddhists recite the five daily recollections, beginning with being subject to aging, sickness and death, as a way to loosen the intoxications of youth, health and life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a lump of salt and a great river, and your line, salt in the river. Did your heart widen once? Today the Buddha remembers his own childhood, in his own words. Day six hundred sixty-one.

We've heard the palace story told about him: the sheltered prince, the four sights. In this short discourse from the Book of Threes, the Buddha tells it himself, and the details are startlingly specific. I was delicate, monks, he says, most delicate. At my father's home, lotus ponds were made just for me, one of blue lotuses, one of red, one of white. I wore only fine cloth from Kasi. A white sunshade was held over me day and night, so cold and heat, dust and dew wouldn't touch me. Today: three intoxications.
screen: `IN HIS OWN WORDS.` → `THREE LOTUS PONDS, BLUE, RED, WHITE.` → `A WHITE SUNSHADE, DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The memory in AN 3.38 keeps going. He had three palaces, one for winter, one for summer, one for the rains. During the rainy months he stayed in the rains palace, entertained by musicians, and didn't come down at all. In other homes, he says, servants were fed broken rice with sour gruel. In his father's house, even the servants ate fine rice and meat. Then the turn. Even with all that, he says, a thought came to me. An untaught person, who is himself subject to aging, sees someone old and feels disgust and shame, forgetting that he will age too. That isn't fitting for me, he thought. And as he reflected, the intoxication of youth left him completely. The same with illness: the untaught are repelled by the sick, though they'll fall ill too. The intoxication of health left him. The same with death. The intoxication of life left him. The Pali word is mada, a word used for drunkenness, for the madness of pride. Youth, health, being alive: none of them are bad. The intoxication is the feeling that they're mine to keep, and that the old, the sick and the dying are some other kind of person. In the very next discourse he names what these three intoxications do. A person drunk on youth, or health, or life, acts badly in body, speech and mind. It's easy to see how: the intoxication whispers that there's plenty of time. Here's what's moving about the discourse. It isn't a lecture on aging. It's a man remembering the white sunshade, and the morning he realized it couldn't keep anything off him forever.
screen: `THREE PALACES, ONE FOR EACH SEASON` · `DISGUST AT THE OLD, FORGETTING ONESELF` · `MADA: DRUNK ON YOUTH, HEALTH, LIFE` · `THE SUNSHADE CAN'T KEEP IT OFF` · then, large: `THE THREE INTOXICATIONS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and feel the body as it is today: the age it is, the health it has, the life that's in it. Let a little gratitude in for each. Then notice, gently, whether any of the three has a grip of pride: I'm too young for that, I never get sick, there's always tomorrow. Choose one, and soften it. Try the plain thought: this too will change. Not with fear. Just with clearer eyes, and kinder ones toward anyone older or sicker than you. The bell holds the time.
Three intoxications. In AN 3.38, the Buddha, remembering his sheltered youth, names the pride of youth, of health, and of life, and tells how each one left him. Today's word.
Your line: the three intoxications. When you see someone older, or ill, today, catch any flinch, and remember: this is my road too. Day six hundred sixty-one.

myth: in AN 3.38 the Buddha tells of his sheltered youth himself
he describes the lotus ponds, the Kasi cloth, the white sunshade and the three palaces.
the discourse says youth, health and life are bad
the intoxication is the problem: the pride that forgets one will age, sicken and die.
the untaught feel disgust at the old, forgetting they will age too
seeing that, the Buddha says, the intoxication of youth left him.

fork.setup: you're a young prince with three palaces and a white sunshade held over you. you see someone old and feel a flash of disgust. what does AN 3.38 say comes next?
options: look away and forget it.
see that you're subject to aging too, and let the pride of youth go.
order the old person out of sight.
fork.reveal: the Buddha says he reflected that disgust wasn't fitting for one who will age, and the intoxication of youth left him.

original.note: Pali mada: intoxication, pride; yobbana-mada, arogya-mada, jivita-mada: of youth, health and life.

trapdoor: what you thought: three intoxications means three kinds of drinking.
what it means: in AN 3.38, the pride of youth, health and life, which makes us forget we too will age, sicken and die.

what a scholar hears: this is one of the rare sutta passages where the Buddha describes his palace youth in the first person; in the suttas the four sights are told of the past buddha Vipassi (DN 14), and many scholars think they were applied to Gotama later, in the commentaries and biographies.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.38 (Sukhumala Sutta; AN 3.39 in some editions)
Anguttara Nikaya 3.39 (Mada Sutta; AN 3.40 in some editions)

662.title: Remember me as awake
662.hook: Dona asks: are you a god? a spirit? a human? No: awake
662.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the Dona story to explain the title buddha, 'the awakened one,' and many Buddhists bow to Buddha images as a sign of respect for that awakening rather than as worship of a god.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the three intoxications, the pride of youth, of health and of life. Did you catch one of them talking? Today a man asks the Buddha what he is, and gets an answer he didn't expect. Day six hundred sixty-two.

A road between two towns. A brahmin named Dona is walking along it, and he stops. In the dust are footprints, and inside each print, the text says, is the mark of a wheel with a thousand spokes, rim and hub complete. Dona knows the old lore about marks like these. These can't be the footprints of an ordinary human being, he thinks. So he follows them, off the road, to the foot of a tree, where someone is sitting cross-legged, still, upright, mindful. Dona walks up and asks a very direct question. Today: remember me as awake.
screen: `FOOTPRINTS IN THE DUST.` → `A WHEEL IN EACH ONE.` → `A FIGURE UNDER A TREE.`

segments.voice: Dona's question comes in four parts. Will you be a god? No, brahmin. A gandhabba, a heavenly musician? No. A yakkha, a spirit of the forest? No. A human being, then? No, brahmin, I will not be a human being. Dona is baffled. Then what will you be? Here the Buddha explains. The things that would make him a god, a spirit or a human, he says, are the taints, the deep habits of craving and confusion that push a being into one kind of life or another. In him those are abandoned, cut at the root like a palm stump, unable to grow again. Then he gives a picture. A blue or red or white lotus is born in the water, grows up in the water, and rises above the water to stand clear of it, and the water doesn't cling to it. In the same way, he says, he was born in the world and grew up in the world, but he has gone beyond the world, and the world doesn't stain him. Then the line. Remember me, brahmin, as a buddha. And buddha is not a name. It's a word everyone in that road understood: awake, the one who has woken up. Notice what the answer refuses. It refuses to be filed under any category Dona brought with him. It doesn't claim divinity, and it doesn't settle for being just another person. It points instead to a state: not asleep. Teachers often use this sutta when someone asks whether Buddhists worship the Buddha as a god. The Buddha's own answer, here, is no.
screen: `A GOD? A SPIRIT? A HUMAN? NO.` · `THE ROOTS ARE CUT.` · `A LOTUS ABOVE THE WATER.` · then, large: `REMEMBER ME AS AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wake up to one moment. Sit, and let your eyes rest. For a few breaths, notice how much of you is half asleep: running a plan, replaying a talk, waiting for the next thing. You don't have to fix it. Then choose one moment, this one, and wake up to it fully. The weight of your body. The air on your skin. The sound nearest you. When you drift, that's fine; the drifting is how you learn what waking feels like. Come back, and wake again. The bell holds the time.
Remember me as awake. The Buddha's answer to Dona in the Numbered Sayings: not a god, not a spirit, not merely human, but buddha, the one who woke up. Today's word.
Your line: remember me as awake. Today, pick one ordinary moment, a door handle, a first sip, a hello, and be fully awake for it. Day six hundred sixty-two.

the one who has woken up

he says no to god, to gandhabba, to yakkha, and even to 'human being.'

born and grown in the world, but not stained by it.
buddha is a family name, like Gotama
Gotama is the clan name; buddha is a title meaning awake.

fork.setup: you're Dona. a stranger sits under a tree, and his footprints carry marks no ordinary person has. what do you do?
options: walk on; it's none of your business.
ask him plainly what kind of being he is.
bow and ask him for a blessing.
fork.reveal: Dona asks straight out: god, spirit or human? the answer to all three is no, and the real answer is a word: awake.

original.note: Pali buddha: past participle of budh, to wake up or to know; 'one who has awakened.'

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha was a man people later turned into a god.
what it means: asked if he was a god, a spirit or a human, he said none of these: he was awake.
what a scholar hears: 'human being' is rejected too, because in the sutta each kind of birth comes from taints that he has cut, 'like a palm stump.'

663.title: The firebrand
663.hook: a torch from a funeral pyre is useless; four kinds of people
663.howItsDone: Many Buddhist teachers describe practice as having two sides, working on one's own mind and serving others, and the firebrand sutta is one of the early texts they cite for holding the two together.

segments.voice: Yesterday Dona asked god, spirit or human, and heard: remember me as awake. Did one ordinary moment get your full attention? Today, a piece of burnt wood. Day six hundred sixty-three.

In ancient India the dead were burned on open pyres at the edge of town. When the fire went down, what was left was a mess: ash, bone, and charred sticks of wood. Picture one of those sticks. Burning at both ends, and in the middle smeared with dung. Nobody would carry it home for the kitchen fire. Nobody would take it into the forest to build with. It's not good for anything, in the village or out of it. The Buddha picks up exactly that stick, in words, and holds it up to a room of monks. Today: the firebrand.
screen: `AFTER THE PYRE.` → `BURNING AT BOTH ENDS.` → `GOOD FOR NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The sutta is in the Book of Fours, and it sorts people into four kinds. The first practices neither for their own good nor for the good of others. That's the firebrand: of no use in the village or the forest. The second practices for the good of others, but not their own. The third practices for their own good, but not for others. The fourth practices for both. Look at the order of the middle two. The Buddha puts the one who works on themselves above the one who works only for others. That can sound selfish, until you think about what 'own good' means here: taming greed, hatred and confusion in yourself. Someone who rushes to fix everyone else while their own temper is on fire can make a lot of smoke. The texts elsewhere give a picture for this: you can't pull someone out of a swamp while you're sinking in it yourself. But the sutta doesn't stop at self. The highest of the four, it says, is the one who practices for both. Then it adds a dairy image. From a cow comes milk, from milk curd, from curd butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee, the finest of all. That cream is the person who works for self and others together. Not first one, then the other. Both, in the same life, in the same day.
screen: `FOUR KINDS OF PEOPLE.` · `THE FIREBRAND: NO USE AT ALL.` · `OWN GOOD ABOVE OTHERS' GOOD ALONE.` · then, large: `THE BEST: FOR SELF AND OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be useful to someone. Sit, and settle for a few breaths. First, the own-good half: notice one thing in you that's smoking right now, a worry, an irritation. Breathe with it, gently, and let it cool a little. Then the others half: bring to mind one person who could use a small, real help today. A message, a dish washed, a question asked and listened to. Picture yourself doing it. Breathe in for yourself. Breathe out for them. The bell holds the time.
The firebrand. In the Numbered Sayings, the stick from a funeral pyre that's useless everywhere: the picture of a life lived for no one's good. Today's word.
Your line: for self and others. Today, do one thing that cools your own fire, and one thing that helps someone else. Both before bed. Day six hundred sixty-three.

highest is the one who works for both self and others.
the firebrand is useless in the village and in the forest
it can't be carried home as fuel or used as timber.
the sutta ends with milk, curd, butter, ghee and cream of ghee
the cream of ghee stands for the person who practices for both.

fork.setup: of the four kinds of people, which does the Buddha call the highest?
options: the one who works only for others.
the one who works for self and others.
the one who works only on themselves.
fork.reveal: the one who practices for both. surprisingly, the sutta puts working on yourself above working only for others, but it ranks both together above everything.

original.note: Pali chavalata: a firebrand from a funeral pyre, from chava, a corpse, and alata, a burning stick.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Buddhism, helping others always comes before yourself.
what it means: AN 4.95 puts working on your own mind above helping others alone, and both together highest.
what a scholar hears: the firebrand image recurs in the canon; in the Itivuttaka a life of grasping and blame is also compared to it.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 8 (Sallekha Sutta), the swamp image

664.title: Together, lives on
664.hook: an old couple, Nakula's parents, wish to meet again in future lives: shared faith, virtue, giving, wisdom
664.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes read the story of Nakula's parents at weddings or in talks on marriage, and many Buddhist couples practice together by keeping precepts, giving and attending the temple as a family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the firebrand from the pyre, and your line, for self and others. Did you manage one of each? Today, two people who did their practice side by side for a lifetime. Day six hundred sixty-four.

Most of the people in the suttas are monks and nuns. These two are not. They're an old married couple from the Bhagga country, known in the texts only as Nakula's father and Nakula's mother. They were married young. One day they come to the Buddha together, and the husband says something remarkable for any marriage, ancient or modern. Since she was brought to me as a girl, he says, I don't know of ever having been unfaithful to her, not even in thought. And his wife says the same of him. Then they ask for something bigger. Today: together, lives on.
screen: `AN OLD MARRIED COUPLE.` → `MARRIED YOUNG.` → `NOT EVEN IN THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Their request is simple and huge. We want to see each other not only in this life, but in lives to come. Is there a way? In the Buddhist picture, life doesn't end at one death, and beings are carried from life to life by what they've done and become. So the couple's question is a real one. And the Buddha takes it seriously. Yes, he says. If a husband and wife both wish to see each other in this life and the next, let them be equal in four things. Equal in faith, the trust that sets you on the path. Equal in virtue, the way you keep your conduct. Equal in generosity, the open hand. Equal in wisdom, seeing how things really are. If those four are shared, he says, they will see each other in this life and in the life to come. Notice what's not on the list. Not looks, not money, not even shared tastes in food. The bond he points to is a shared practice, two people walking the same way at the same pace. And it's a list you can actually work on together. Elsewhere in the Numbered Sayings, the Buddha names Nakula's father and mother as foremost among his lay followers in one quality: trust, the kind of closeness people can lean on. A rare honor for a pair, and a rare portrait in the early texts of a happy marriage held up as a model.
screen: `MEET AGAIN IN LIVES TO COME.` · `SAME FAITH, SAME VIRTUE.` · `SAME GIVING, SAME WISDOM.` · then, large: `TOGETHER, LIVES ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share a practice with a loved one. Sit for a few breaths and bring to mind someone close: a partner, a parent, a friend, a sibling. Picture their face. Now go through the four, gently. Is there something you both trust in? A way of behaving you both care about? A way you both like to give? Something you've both come to understand? Pick one. Think of a small way to do it together this week: a walk, a meal shared out, a quiet ten minutes side by side. The bell holds the time.
Together. Nakula's parents, the old couple of the Numbered Sayings, and the four things the Buddha said keep two lives side by side: faith, virtue, giving and wisdom, shared. Today's word.
Your line: together, lives on. Today, ask someone you love to do one small good thing with you, and do it side by side. Day six hundred sixty-four.

pairs: the trust that sets you on the path
foremost in trust among lay followers

myth: the Buddha told the couple that married love ends at death
he told them how they could meet again: share faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom.
looks and wealth are on the Buddha's list of four
the four are faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom.
the couple were lay followers, not monks or nuns
a householder couple from the Bhagga country.

fork.setup: an old couple asks: how can we see each other again in lives to come? what does the Buddha say?
options: it can't be done; let go of each other.
be equal in faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom.
make a vow before an image of the Buddha.
fork.reveal: he gives them four things to share. the answer isn't a vow or a farewell, but a practice they can do together.

original.note: Pali samasaddha: 'of the same faith,' the first of four; the sutta goes on: same virtue, same giving, same wisdom.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism is mostly about leaving your family behind.
what it means: the Buddha told a married couple how to stay together, even across lives.
what a scholar hears: the sutta's name, samajivina, means 'living in harmony,' and the four 'sames' are its formula.

665.title: Five remembrances
665.hook: I will age, sicken, die, be parted from what I love, and I am heir to my deeds
665.howItsDone: Many Buddhist monasteries and lay groups recite the five remembrances, often daily, as part of morning or evening chanting, and teachers offer them as a reflection for anyone, ordained or not.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an old couple, and four things shared so they could stay together, lives on. Did you do one good thing side by side with someone? Today closes a week, with five lines to say to yourself. Day six hundred sixty-five.

Look back at this week. The gold-washer, refining slowly. Salt lost in the river. The three intoxications: youth, health and life. Dona, and remember me as awake. The firebrand. And the old couple, together. Now, four days ago, those three intoxications came with a quiet warning: the pride of being young, of being well, of being alive makes people careless. Today's sutta is the medicine for that pride. It's short enough to fit on a card. The Buddha says these five things should be reflected on often, by everyone: man or woman, householder or monk. Today: five remembrances.

segments.voice: Here are the five, in plain words. One: I am of the nature to age; I haven't gone beyond aging. Two: I am of the nature to get sick; I haven't gone beyond sickness. Three: I am of the nature to die; I haven't gone beyond death. Four: everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I will be parted from them. Five: I am the owner of my deeds, heir to my deeds, born of my deeds, bound to my deeds; whatever I do, good or bad, I will inherit it. Now the surprise. This sounds grim, and the sutta knows it. So it explains why each line helps. Thinking on aging, it says, wears down the pride of youth. Thinking on sickness wears down the pride of health. Thinking on death wears down the pride of being alive. Thinking on parting wears down the clinging to what's dear. And thinking on deeds wears down misconduct in body, speech and mind. The first four are about what you can't control. The fifth is about the one thing you can. That's the turn. You can't stop the clock or keep everyone forever. But what you do today becomes what you inherit. Heir is the key word: like an estate, your deeds are passed down to you, the good with the bad. Many Buddhists, in monasteries and at home, still recite these five, often daily.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite the five. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then, slowly, one line per few breaths, say them inwardly. I will grow old. I may grow ill. I will die. What I love will change, and I will part from it. I am heir to my deeds. If a line feels heavy, stay with the breath until it softens. Let the last line land as a kind of relief: there is something here that's yours to shape. The bell holds the time.
Five remembrances. Aging, sickness, death, parting, and deeds: the five things the Buddha asked everyone to reflect on often, to wear down pride and steady the hand. Today's word.
Your line: heir to my deeds. Today, before one choice, small or large, ask: is this something I'd like to inherit? Day six hundred sixty-five.
